data.text/markdown:
Odometry uncertainty: Gaussian vs. particles

A robot drives with noisy wheel odometry, so the uncertainty in its pose grows at every step. This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to propagate that uncertainty in SE(2) in two ways:
  • Linearized Gaussian: Gaussian poses composed with first-order (Jacobian) error propagation, as an EKF does.
  • Monte Carlo: thousands of particles, each moved with its own random odometry error, as a particle filter does.
It uses these MRPT modules:
  • mrpt.obs: the probabilistic odometry motion model (CActionRobotMovement2D).
  • mrpt.poses: poses and Gaussian pose PDFs (CPose2D, CPose3D, CPose3DPDFGaussian).
  • mrpt.slam and mrpt.bayes: a particle filter (CMonteCarloLocalization2D, CParticleFilter).
Move the sliders: with little heading noise both methods agree, but with long paths and large heading noise the particles bend into a "banana" that no ellipse can describe.

data.text/html: Parameters (each step: 0.5 m forward, then turn)

data.text/markdown:
1. The motion model

At each step the odometry reads the same increment: 0.5 m forward plus the turn. MRPT's Gaussian motion model turns that reading into a PDF over the true increment, whose standard deviations grow with the distance ||(d||) traveled: ||(\sigma_{xy} = a_1 d||) and ||(\sigma_\phi = a_3 d||).

Per-step increment, as a CPosePDFGaussian:

Covariance:

2. Linearized Gaussian propagation

If the pose at step ||(k-1||) is Gaussian, ||(\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k-1}, \Sigma_{k-1})||), composing it with the increment ||(u \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar u, \Sigma_u)||) gives ||[\mu_k = \mu_{k-1} \oplus \bar u, \qquad \Sigma_k = J_1 \Sigma_{k-1} J_1^\top + J_2 \Sigma_u J_2^\top,||]with ||(J_1, J_2||) the Jacobians of the composition ||(\oplus||). The + operator of CPose3DPDFGaussian implements this. A planar pose is just a 3D pose with ||(z||), pitch and roll equal to zero, so we lift the 2D increment to 3D.

3. Monte Carlo propagation

A particle filter without observations only runs its prediction step: each particle is composed with its own random sample of the increment, so no linearization is involved. CParticleFilter.executeOn() does that on a CMonteCarloLocalization2D particle set when no observation is given.

data.text/markdown:
What to look at
  • The Gaussian mean stays on the noise-free path, while the particle mean is pulled to the inner side of the banana: the mean of a curved distribution is not on the curve.
  • The ellipse has roughly the right spread, but it cannot bend: it covers poses that no particle reached, and misses particles on the tips.
  • Heading noise is what bends the cloud, and the error it causes grows with the distance traveled. Set a small heading noise and the two methods agree.

Run it on your computer (Linux, Python 3.11 to 3.14): 
uvx marimo edit --sandbox https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MRPT/mrpt-notebooks/main/notebooks/pose_uncertainty.py
